summary: Discovery workshop to decide between Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, or Private for CedarPoint Health. Focus: p95 latency SLOs for streaming chat, steady-state tokens/sec, concurrency, and benchmark plan. Security/regulatory gating discussed (HIPAA, KMS, audit logs).
topics: p95 token latency vs response latency
streaming first-token latency and steady-state throughput
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-05-18 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~62m | Recording: Zoom
Attendees: Liam Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nandakumar (Redwood SE), Sara Mitchell (Head of Platform, CedarPoint), Dr. Aaron Bell (CTO), Noah Park (Infra), Lena Ortiz (Security), Tariq (ML Lead)

Summary: quick recap at top, we want to hit p95 goals for live chat with PHI, test hosted and dedicated latencies, figure out if private deploy is required for regulated flows.

00:00 Liam: okay everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call. we're going to run through your production profile and then outline a benchmarking plan.
00:23 Sara: thanks, yep, planning to replace our current rule-based triage with streaming chat, typical session is 1–2k tokens, bursts of ~500 concurrent endusers at peak.
00:42 Priya: when you say 500 concurrent endusers, is that concurrent open streaming sessions or TTF (time to first) requests?
00:50 Sara: open streams, like active websocket sessions. typical question length 40–80 tokens, but we also have a smaller subset that sends long clinical notes ~1,200 tokens.
01:08 Dr. Aaron: the hard SLO is p95 end-to-end for message generation under 400ms for short interactions; for long notes we're more flexible (p95 < 2s). Those short SLOs are non-negotiable for real-time triage.
01:28 Liam: got it — so you want streaming first-token and mid-stream p95 under 400ms for 40–80 token replies. that's tight but achievable. what are your current infra and routing?
01:41 Noah: currently on EKS in us-east-1, we pre-warm pools with node autoscaler. we run a mix of CPU-only for some microservices and a ML cluster for model inference on dedicated gpus in a different account. cross-account peering is limited.
02:10 Priya: two quick things that drive p95: contiguous batching and KV cache effectiveness. if you have a lot of unique prefixes (clinical notes) warmup is low and p95 degrades. do you have repeated prefixes?
02:26 Tariq: clinical notes are mostly unique, but templates are reused maybe 30% of the time. we saw cache hit rates ~18% on our internal prototype.
02:37 Priya: yeah that matters — with low KV hit you lose the benefit of prefix caching and token/sec drops, p95 rises. for streaming the runtime also optimizes for first-token path; we can route to smaller context variants for short replies to keep latency low.
03:05 Sara: can you explain that routing option? we don't want to sacrifice quality.
03:10 Liam: sure — Redwood can pin policy to route short-context requests to a cheaper/low-latency model variant (e.g., 4k -> 2k context), with fallback to the full model if quality check fails. it's automatic and can be conservative.
03:32 Dr. Aaron: how do you quantify the p95 when batching is happening? our traffic is bursty so batching helps cost but hurts tail latency if not controlled.
03:44 Priya: we provide two knobs: max batch latency and target batch size. when you need tail guarantees we lower max batch latency which reduces batching efficiency but improves p95. in dedicated you can also reserve capacity so batching is predictable.
04:10 Noah: so hosted can do it but dedicated buys us predictable p95? what's the delta we should expect?
04:18 Liam: ballpark: for short streaming responses at moderate concurrency (100–300 streams) hosted p95 can be ~350–500ms depending on region/hotness; dedicated with pinned pools and local GPUs can often reach ~200–350ms p95 for the same load, because we avoid noisy neighbor effects and can tailor kernel selection.
04:42 Sara: and private on-prem? we want to consider private if latency still fluctuates and for PHI rules.
04:49 Priya: private gives you full control but adds ops overhead. it also changes the kernel throughput depending on your GPU infra (A100, H100, or lower). for on-prem H100s we can get strong token/sec but you need to manage driver/kernels.
05:10 Lena: on compliance — we need SOC 2, audit logs, KMS integration, and attestation that PHI isn't logged in hosted. is that in your docs?
05:20 Liam: yes we'll send SOC2 and our security whitepaper. hosted can be configured to not persist logs and to integrate with customer KMS via envelope encryption. we also support private where keys never leave your KMS.
05:32 Lena: ok please include network diagrams and exact retention controls.
05:38 Liam: will do.
05:42 06:00 Priya: back to benchmarking — realistic plan is: you give us the 2k prompt set, the load profile (peak concurrency, arrival distribution), and we'll run three tests: hosted baseline, dedicated reserved pool, and a private dry-run if you can provide infra access. each test records per-token times, first-token latency, p95/p99, and tokens/sec steady-state.
06:23 Tariq: we can provide the prompt set. our traffic shape is spiky: 30s bursts every 3–5 minutes with background of ~50 rps. peak~500 open streams.
06:36 Priya: perfect. for the hosted benchmark we'll set your region to us-east-1 and pin a model variant optimized for lower latency (we'll share exact model and quantization). for dedicated we suggest reserving 2–4 GPUs to start depending on measured tokens/sec.
07:02 Dr. Aaron: can you give some initial tokens/sec numbers to size dedicated?
07:10 Priya: rough numbers (very approximate): an H100 int8-ish path might do 2500–3800 tokens/sec per GPU for steady-state on a medium-size model; a4-like variants are different. these numbers degrade with longer contexts and with KV misses. so if you have lots of long clinical notes expect lower aggregate throughput.
07:35 Liam: to convert to users — if average reply 60 tokens, 1 GPU at 3000 tokens/sec supports ~50 concurrent streams with average turn times, but with streaming and per-token overhead you want headroom. for 500 concurrent streams you'd be looking at around 8–12 GPUs depending on hot/cold distribution and batching policy.
08:05 Noah: that's a useful back-of-envelope. so we should test with 2, 8, and 12 GPU configs in dedicated to find the knee.
08:14 Priya: exactly — and we'll run warmup phases to exercise KV cache; measure cache hit vs cold-start impact. also instrument p95 per-client so we can see variance across streams.
08:29 Sara: on the topic of streaming p95, are you reporting token-level p95 or response-level? which should we use for SLO?
08:39 Liam: we generally report both. industry standard for interactive SLO is p95 for first meaningful token and p95 for full response time. for your 400ms target you should use first-token p95 for short replies.
08:58 Tariq: any differences in behavior between hosted and dedicated when using streaming websockets vs our own multiplexed gRPC?
09:08 Priya: not much in the runtime; the transport affects connection lifecycle and TLS overhead. we recommend websocket streaming for browser apps. if you have a multiplexed gRPC fanout that reduces connection churn and is fine. we will measure transport overhead in benchmarking.
09:31 Dr. Aaron: security again — for hosted, how do you guarantee PHI never leaves our VPC?
09:38 Liam: hosted cannot run inside your VPC; you can either use VPC peering + private link to reduce exposure, or choose Dedicated with private link and VPC options, or full Private deployment where control plane runs inside your VPC/on-prem. we'll outline network patterns.
09:58 Lena: for auditing, we need immutable audit logs with export to our SIEM and a retention policy. do you support that in hosted?
10:07 Liam: yes hosted can stream audit logs to your logging endpoint, and Dedicated/Private give you more direct control. we'll include a sample log schema.
10:20 Sara: what about rollback/fallback — if a dedicated pool is overloaded, can we fallback to hosted automatically?
10:28 Priya: yes, smart routing can failover to a compatible open model in hosted tier; you can set cost vs latency policy. but for PHI flows you'd likely want to disable automatic fallback and instead trigger degraded mode.
10:47 Dr. Aaron: important — we cannot send PHI to hosted under any circumstance. That means dedicated or private for those flows.
10:55 Liam: understood — then hosted could still be used for non-PHI conversational features, or as a failover with sanitized payloads. we'll document interplay.
11:08 Noah: about quantization — any pitfalls? we've seen hallucination changes when moving to int8.
11:14 Priya: quantization does sometimes affect numeric accuracy and some safety filters; for short replies it's often acceptable, but for critical clinical text we recommend higher-precision variants, or a small eval suite to check regression. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization per workload.
11:40 Tariq: will the benchmarking pipeline include regression checks? we need to ensure quality doesn't degrade below our baseline.
11:47 Priya: yes — we'll run quality probes using a small eval set you provide. if a quantized variant falls beyond thresholds we won't recommend it.
12:00 Sara: what about cost estimates for dedicated? we need a monthly number with committed capacity.
12:08 Liam: we'll produce a committed capacity quote: a range based on GPUs (start with 4 GPUs for testing, 8–12 for production peak). we'll show cost per 1M tokens for hosted and cost amortized for dedicated.
12:25 Dr. Aaron: can you give us a recommended SLA for p95 on dedicated?
12:32 Priya: we typically target p95 SLOs with 99.9% uptime for Dedicated customers; exact p95 number is driven by pool sizing and configuration. for your 400ms target we'd bake in reservation, local region placement, and lower batch latency.
12:50 13:05 Noah: for the benchmark harness, what load generator do you recommend?
13:11 Priya: we can share a JMeter/Torch-based generator we use internally. it'll simulate websocket streams with your exact arrival patterns and will report per-token latencies.
13:24 Sara: nice. let's talk schedule — can we run hosted baseline next Wednesday?
13:30 Liam: yes, Priya availability?
13:34 Priya: available, I'll coordinate with Noah for peering and keys.
13:38 Liam: great. I'll send invites and the checklist.
13:42 14:00 Lena: last question: automatic retention of prompts for debug — can we opt-out? we need a no-retain policy for PHI.
14:09 Liam: yes, we support no-persist mode and trimmed debug logs that keep only non-PHI metadata. we'll document how to enable it per route.
14:22 Sara: ok thanks. can you also include sample dashboard screenshots for per-route cost and latency so our execs can see impact?
14:29 Liam: yes we'll attach Redwood Console screenshots.
14:33 14:40 Priya: recap of next steps: we run hosted baseline, run dedicated sizing tests, share security docs, and prepare cost quote. Priya will run token/sec baseline; Noah will provide infra details; Lena will provide compliance list.
14:54 Liam: Perfect. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites and the doc pack.
15:02 End of call.

Notes about transcription: occasional overlap and mis-attribution (Speaker labels approximate). Some technical terms transcribed as K V cache or H one zero zero (H100) in places.
